design_detail: Literature review with a documented search but narrative synthesis, funded through NIDA Clinical Trials Network node grants and acknowledging the support of the Network's Gender Special Interest Group. Medline and PsycInfo were searched for English-language articles from January 1975 to September 2005 with listed terms, and reference lists were checked; 2,474 Medline and 636 PsycInfo records were screened on title and abstract for relevance by three authors, leaving 280 relevant articles (11.8% randomized trials, 7.9% non-randomized or quasi-experimental trials, 31.2% prospective cohorts). The text discusses adult studies from 1990–2005 on treatment entry, retention, outcome, and women-only against mixed-gender treatment. Excluded: epidemiology of women's substance use, adolescents, criminal-justice populations, nicotine treatment, and studies with substance outcomes as secondary outcomes; pregnancy studies are in the supplement only. No eligibility criteria beyond relevance, no appraisal of the included studies and no pooling; the study-level table is an online supplement that was not read. Classed as a narrative review rather than a systematic review for these reasons, although the authors describe the review as systematic and critical.
can_establish: What the published literature to September 2005 on adult women in substance use treatment contained (mostly observational, 11.8% randomized) and what its larger studies showed about gender differences in entering treatment, staying in it and its outcomes, with the primary studies to consult.
cannot_establish: The size of any gender difference (nothing is pooled); whether women-only or gender-specific programmes cause better outcomes (few randomized comparisons, with mixed results); anything about adolescents, pregnant women, criminal-justice populations or nicotine treatment (excluded); or findings after 2005.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (literature review). Medline and PsycInfo, January 1975 to September 2005, English only, with reference-list searching (1.1 Search Method).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Relevance to treatment entry, retention or outcome in women, from women-only samples or gender comparisons in mixed samples; literature reviews, meta-analyses and theoretical papers also included. Excluded: general characteristics and epidemiology, adolescents, pregnant women (supplement only), criminal-justice populations, nicotine, and studies where substance outcomes were secondary (1. Introduction, 3rd and 4th paragraphs).
sample.selection_effects: English only; PsycInfo restricted to subject headings; screening by relevance without stated criteria or duplicate decisions. Almost all outcome and retention data come from people who entered treatment, so they describe women and men in treatment, not everyone with a disorder; the review notes that treatment-entry findings depend on the time since onset and on how treatment is defined.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level. For the gender differences in treatment entry, the review names the sample: population surveys (NLAES 1992, described as a retrospective cohort analysis of one cross-sectional survey, so onset and treatment were reported after the fact; the 1999 and 2002 national household surveys, past-year treatment; a three-country survey with a broad definition of help-seeking) and clinical or community cohorts (an 8-year prospective follow-up of initially untreated drinkers; HMO and programme cohorts). For the faster progression of women to treatment stated in the Introduction, the samples, timing measures and adjustments are not described.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed, apart from use of multiple drugs as a gender-specific predictor of outcome in one cited study.

comparison.controls: Men compared with women in mixed-gender samples; within-women comparisons by characteristics; women-only against mixed-gender programmes.

outcomes.instruments: As in the cited studies (for example the Addiction Severity Index, self-reported abstinence, relapse, sessions attended, length of stay, completion); not standardized across studies.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors note that retention and completion are defined in many different ways (dichotomous session or day thresholds, continuous length of stay, completion of a planned course), which hampers comparison (3. Characteristics Associated with Substance Abuse Treatment Retention and Completion, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Recovery outcomes are taken as each study defined them, for example abstinence in the past 30 days at a 6- or 7-month follow-up, relapse, days abstinent, or decreases in drinking over five years; time windows range from 12 weeks to five years and nearly all participants had treatment.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited; none pooled. Ever treated for alcohol use disorders in NLAES 1992 (7,359 people with alcohol abuse or dependence): 23% of men vs 15.1% of women; cumulative probability of treatment by 30 years after onset .424 vs .356; no difference in the first 8 years; men 13%–20% more likely between 8 and 25 years. Past-year alcohol treatment among people with alcohol dependence (1999 household survey, 32,628 people): 12.5% of women vs 12.1% of men. Retention in large multi-programme data sets: very few gender differences (for example men 20% less likely than women to stay 90 days in outpatient drug-free care among 10,010 patients). Abstinence at 6 months in older adults: 79.3% of women vs 54% of men, not significant after adjustment for length of stay.
analysis.selective_reporting: The text discusses studies from 1990 to 2005 selected from the 280 without a stated rule; the full study-by-study results are only in the supplement. Results are otherwise reported in both directions, including null and unfavourable findings for women-only treatment.
analysis.power: Not applicable at review level; the authors note that few outcome studies had samples large enough to test gender by race, ethnicity or age.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In one national US survey, women with alcohol use disorders were less likely than men to have ever been treated, a gap that appeared only more than eight years after onset and was absent in the most severe cases; past-year and broadly defined help-seeking showed no gender difference, and for illicit drugs one national survey found none. Small clinical studies of retention disagree; large multi-programme data sets show few gender differences, which where present favour women. Most outcome studies find no gender difference and those that find one mostly favour women. Randomized comparisons of women-only with mixed-gender treatment are few and mixed, and the one comparing outcomes favoured a hospital mixed-gender programme on abstinence over the women-only programme, which did not differ from two community mixed-gender programmes.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that a convergence of evidence shows women are less likely over the lifetime to enter treatment, and that once in treatment gender is not a significant predictor of retention, completion or outcome. Gaps: (1) the lifetime treatment-entry conclusion rests chiefly on one survey of alcohol use disorders (Dawson, 1996) together with sex ratios in treatment facilities; for illicit drugs the population data cited show no gender effect, and the alcohol gap depends on time since onset and severity; (2) the Introduction states as established, without counter-evidence, that women progress faster from use to regular use to first treatment for alcohol, opioid and cannabis dependence (the sentence before gives the label of a most reproducible finding to women's vulnerability to adverse medical and social consequences, and the paragraph's last sentence folds faster progression into that vulnerability), citing six studies, among them treatment samples and Dawson (1996), whose results as described in section 2.3 do not show earlier treatment entry for women; (3) 'not a significant predictor' summarizes mostly observational studies of people already in treatment, with varied outcome definitions, and is not an equivalence result. The authors are otherwise careful: they call the evidence base the very earliest stage, say women-only treatment is not necessarily more effective, and describe the subgroup interventions as early-stage.

timeline.event: Piazza, Vrbka and Yeager describe telescoping in women in treatment (cited in the Introduction).
Dawson's analysis of NLAES 1992: lifetime alcohol treatment 23% of men vs 15.1% of women with alcohol abuse or dependence (as described in this review).
Project MATCH telescoping study, cited in the Introduction for faster progression in women.

Randomized comparison of a women-only day programme with three mixed-gender programmes; the only difference favoured a hospital mixed-gender programme on total abstinence, with no difference from the two community programmes (Kaskutas et al., 2005, as described in this review).
General-population analysis of two US surveys: men had higher hazards of dependence and of treatment, and the full telescoping pattern was not found.
The same group's update (search terms reused): women and men do not substantively differ in treatment outcomes, smoking cessation excepted.

replication.where_it_stands: Its central conclusions (no substantive gender difference in retention or outcome once in treatment; women-only settings not by themselves more effective) were restated by the same group in 2018 (mchugh_2018). Its telescoping statement predates the general-population test (keyes_2010), which did not find the full pattern.

what_would_settle_it: For treatment entry, a prospective population cohort with linked treatment records recording when men and women first meet criteria and first receive treatment; for treatment effects, the trial the authors propose: one standard treatment delivered in men-only, women-only and mixed-gender groups with randomization, standard outcome definitions and enough women to test interactions with age, race and co-occurring disorders.

domains.note: Two databases, dates, terms, reference lists and record counts are reported and screening was by three authors; but English only, relevance was the only stated criterion, duplicate decisions are not described, and the studies discussed were chosen from the 280 without a stated rule.

No formal appraisal, though designs and sample sizes are given, larger representative studies are weighted over small clinical ones, and some limits are named (broad help-seeking definitions; small samples; non-random assignment to programmes).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Several studies central to the entry, retention and outcome sections are the authors' own (Green et al.; Greenfield et al.; Hien et al.).
Suggested explanations are marked as such ('may', 'it has been suggested'), and the summaries state the limits of the evidence.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on gender differences in treatment entry, retention and outcome
domains.note: Findings in both directions are given, including null results and a trial favouring a mixed-gender programme; only the Introduction's statement on faster progression in women omits counter-evidence.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist gives some concerns, set by the partly systematic selection, the absence of appraisal and reliance on the authors' studies. AMSTAR 2 was not used because the review has no eligibility criteria beyond relevance, no assessment of the included studies and no synthesis method, and its study-level table is in an unread supplement. The review may be cited for the state of this literature to 2005, for its summary that gender did not predict retention or outcome among people in treatment, and as a guide to the primary studies (Dawson, 1996, for lifetime treatment entry; the large multi-programme retention studies; the randomized programme comparisons), whose figures should be cited from the primary papers where possible. Its Introduction's statement on faster progression in women should not be cited without the sample caveat.

key_findings.finding: Search: Medline and PsycInfo, January 1975 to September 2005, English only, with reference lists checked; 2,474 Medline and 636 PsycInfo records, screened by three authors for relevance, gave 280 relevant articles, 90% from 1990 or later (43.9% of those since 2000). 11.8% were randomized trials, 7.9% non-randomized or quasi-experimental trials and 31.2% prospective cohorts.
key_findings.locator: 1.1 Search Method; 1.2 Search Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The Introduction states that women advance more rapidly than men from use to regular use to first treatment for alcohol, opioid and cannabis dependence and arrive with equal severity despite fewer years of use and smaller quantities, citing mainly treatment-sample studies (Piazza et al., 1989; Randall et al., 1999; Hernandez-Avila et al., 2004) together with Dawson (1996); it adds that age of initiation is roughly equal between the sexes in younger cohorts.
key_findings.note: No sample type, timing measure or adjustment is described for these studies; see reporting issue 2 on Dawson (1996).

key_findings.finding: Women are under-represented in treatment relative to their share of disorders: men to women 3.3:1 in US alcohol treatment facilities in 1991 against 2.7:1 for alcohol use disorders in the population; 2.3:1 in US facilities in 2002 against 1.9:1 for past-year alcohol dependence and 1.5:1 for illicit drug dependence (2003 NSDUH); in Australia 2:1 for high-risk drinking against 3:1 to 10:1 in alcohol services. Women with problem drinking more often seek help in non-specialist settings, especially mental-health services.
key_findings.locator: 2.1 Gender Disparities among Participants in Substance Abuse Treatment; 2.2 Gender Disparities in Choice of Treatment Service Sectors

key_findings.finding: Lifetime treatment entry in a general-population sample (NLAES 1992; 7,359 people with alcohol abuse or dependence; retrospective cohort analysis): 23% of men and 15.1% of women had ever been treated (physician, counsellor, Alcoholics Anonymous, other professional or treatment facility); cumulative probability of treatment by 30 years after onset .424 in men and .356 in women; no gender difference up to 8 years after onset; men 13%–20% more likely to start treatment between 8 and 25 years after onset; no gender difference among the most severely dependent; the male-to-female ratio fell from 1.75:1 with one symptom to 1.24:1 with 15 symptoms (Dawson, 1996).
key_findings.locator: 2.3 Gender Disparities in Treatment Entry and Ever Receiving Treatment, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Shorter windows and broader definitions show no gender difference in treatment entry: past-year alcohol treatment among people with alcohol dependence 12.5% of women vs 12.1% of men (1999 household survey, 32,628 people; specialty care 5.7% vs 4.3%, non-specialty 6.8% vs 7.7%); no difference in services over 8 years among 230 women and 236 men who were untreated at the start; gender not associated with past-year use of substance-use services (2002 NSDUH); no gender difference in ever seeking help in a three-country survey that counted telling any professional or attending self-help (50–85% help-seeking). Among 248 inner-city women in Puerto Rico with cocaine or heroin dependence, 36.6% had ever been treated.

Documented barriers for women include pregnancy and fear of losing custody or of prosecution, childcare, economic barriers, co-occurring mood, eating, anxiety and post-traumatic disorders, trauma histories, lack of partner or family support, stigma, and lower perceived need for treatment.
key_findings.locator: 2.4 Specific Barriers to Treatment Entry for Women, 1st–5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Retention: up to 50% of people in treatment drop out within the first month; small clinical studies disagree (five found more dropout in women, two less, one a complex pattern, others none); large multi-programme data sets show very few gender differences, for example 10,010 patients in 96 programmes (men 20% less likely to stay 90 days in outpatient drug-free care) and 26,047 patients in 87 Los Angeles programmes (where differences appeared, women more often completed), and in the Alcohol and Drug Services Study (4,689 adults, 1,239 women) gender was not associated with completion after adjustment.
key_findings.locator: 3. Characteristics Associated with Substance Abuse Treatment Retention and Completion, 1st paragraph; 3.1 Gender Differences in Treatment Retention, 1st, 5th and 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Programme features: in the Alcohol and Drug Services Study, women-only facilities or on-site childcare were not associated with completion but were positively correlated with length of stay; in a randomized trial, women who kept one or two children with them in residential treatment stayed significantly longer, a result confirmed in a quasi-experimental study.
key_findings.locator: 3.3 Program-Related Characteristics Associated with Treatment Retention in Women, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Outcomes: many studies find few or no gender differences; where differences appear, women generally do better. Examples: 567 women and 506 men treated for methamphetamine use, greater improvement in women in family and medical problems at 3 and 9 months; a Dutch trial of 34 women and 29 men with crack cocaine dependence, longer abstinence in women; older adults in outpatient alcohol treatment, 79.3% of women vs 54% of men abstinent in the past 30 days at 6 months, a difference that disappeared after adjusting for length of stay, although women had no heavy-drinking days in the past month at 6 months against an average of four for men; five-year follow-up of treatment and community samples, women more likely to decrease drinking; a meta-analysis of seven brief-intervention studies in primary care, no gender difference.
key_findings.locator: 4.1 Substance Abuse Outcomes versus Predictors of Outcomes, 1st–5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: In an HMO outpatient programme, women who completed treatment were more than nine times as likely as other women to be abstinent for 30 days at 7-month follow-up, men who completed about three times as likely as other men.
key_findings.locator: 4.4 Effects of Treatment Retention and Completion on Substance Abuse Outcomes, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Co-occurring psychiatric disorders generally predict poorer outcomes in both sexes, with sex-specific patterns that vary between studies; 30–50% of people with bulimia and 12–18% with anorexia had a concurrent alcohol or drug use disorder, and no treatment outcome studies for this combination existed.
key_findings.locator: 4.2 Co-occurring Psychiatric Disorders and Substance Abuse Outcomes Following Treatment, 2nd, 3rd and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: In a nine-site quasi-experimental study, 1,023 women with co-occurring disorders and histories of violence in integrated, trauma-informed services improved more in PTSD symptoms and drug use and problem severity at six months than 983 women in usual care.

Women-only against mixed-gender treatment: a meta-analysis (Orwin et al., 2001) found single-gender treatment effective, most strongly for pregnancy outcomes, with small improvements in alcohol and drug use, but few of its studies compared women-only with mixed-gender programmes. Randomized comparisons: no difference in refusal or 25-day attrition (Condelli et al., 2000); higher retention in a women-only day programme for women with prenatally exposed infants (Strantz and Welch, 1995); in Kaskutas et al. (2005), the only significant difference was higher total abstinence in a hospital-based mixed-gender programme, which cost twice as much per week, than in the women-only programme, which did not differ from the two community-based mixed-gender programmes (small sample; the review concludes that women may be equally well served by high-quality mixed-gender and women-only day programmes). Non-randomized comparisons were null (Bride, 2001; Copeland et al., 1993) or favoured women-only programmes on days in treatment and completion (Grella, 1999).
key_findings.locator: 5. Gender-Specific Versus Mixed-Gender Treatment Services, 1st paragraph; 5.2 Comparisons of Women-Only versus Mixed-Gender Treatment Settings, 1st–6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Preferences: in a study of women's treatment needs that the review calls quasi-experimental (Swift and Copeland, 1996), women who had attended women-only programmes generally endorsed them; 42% of the women surveyed had no strong feelings for or against mixed-gender programmes, while 11% felt uncomfortable or unsafe in them, 10% found male clients arrogant or sexist and 6% felt harassed or dominated.
key_findings.locator: 5.3 Potential Effective Elements in Women-Only Treatment, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Authors' conclusions: about 12% of studies were randomized and the evidence base is at its earliest stage; women with substance use disorders are less likely than men to enter treatment over the lifetime; gender is not necessarily a predictor of retention, completion or outcome once treatment begins; changing a programme to women-only does not by itself change outcomes, while interventions for specific subgroups of women show promise in small or non-randomized studies.
key_findings.locator: 6. Summary of Findings and Implications, 1st–4th and 6th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The address of the supplementary results table is left as a placeholder ('doi:xxxxxxxx' in the Introduction and 'doi:xxxxxxxxx' in footnote 1); PMC holds the supplement as a spreadsheet file, which was not opened.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), 1. Introduction, 2nd paragraph; Footnotes; Supplementary Material
reporting_issues.consequence: The study-by-study results for the 280 articles were not read, so the counts by design and the completeness of the narrative selection cannot be checked from the card.

reporting_issues.issue: The Introduction cites Dawson (1996) among studies showing that women advance faster than men to first treatment, but section 2.3 reports the same study as finding no gender difference in treatment entry for 8 years after onset and higher entry in men from 8 to 25 years.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), 1. Introduction, 1st paragraph; 2.3, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: Dawson (1996) should not be cited for faster treatment entry in women without reading it; the review's own account points the other way.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 3.1 first counts four studies with no gender difference in retention (Fiorentine et al., 1997; Green et al., 2002; Mertens and Weisner, 2000; Veach et al., 2000), then says three, describing Fiorentine et al. (1997) separately as finding more group sessions attended by women.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), 3.1 Gender Differences in Treatment Retention, 1st and 4th paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the tally of small retention studies is approximate.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and section 6 present the 90%, about 40% and 11.8% (about 12%) figures as shares of studies investigating gender differences in treatment outcomes, while section 1.2 gives them for all 280 relevant articles, which include reviews, theoretical papers and women-only studies.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Abstract; 1.2 Search Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; 6. Summary, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The share of randomized trials refers to the 280 relevant articles as a whole.

reporting_issues.issue: Editing slips: the Alcohol and Drug Services Study is abbreviated both ADDS and ADSS, and Fiorentine and Hillhouse (1999) is described twice in nearly identical words (4.5, 4th paragraph; 5.3, 2nd paragraph).

A demonstration project (Roberts and Nishimoto, 1996) is described as randomly assigning patients to a women-focused day programme or a traditional outpatient programme, but the completion result reported compares the day programme with a residential programme for women and their children and a traditional residential programme.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), 3.3 Program-Related Characteristics Associated with Treatment Retention in Women, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The description does not hang together; the design and the comparison should be taken from the primary paper, not from this review.
